statement: h(theta) <= eta_theta(0) - eta_theta(delta) for every delta != 0 (averaged margin, network-level analogue of Morwani's eta_{u,v,w})
evidence:
Source: Morwani, Edelman, Oncescu, Zhao, Kakade, "Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks", ICLR 2024 Spotlight, arXiv:2311.07568v2. I fetched the HTML and the abs page and grepped them.

What they prove:
- Sec 3.2 "Multi-Class Classification" defines the class-weighted margin for any weighting tau(x,y) over the wrong labels: g'(theta,x,y) = f(theta,x)[y] - sum_{y' != y} tau(x,y)[y'] f(theta,x)[y'].
- Same section, verbatim: "Note that g'(theta,x,y) >= g(theta,x,y) as g' replaces the max by a weighted sum."
- q* is uniform on the data (Sec 3.3, step 1).
- App. F.1 (proof of Thm 7) defines, for a single neuron, eta_{u,v,w}(delta) := E_{a,b}[(u(a)+v(b))^2 w(a+b-delta)]. It maximises eta(0) - E_{delta != 0} eta(delta) (Eq. 4) with uniform tau(a,b)[c'] = 1/(p-1).

Why our lemma is a specialisation: lem:avg is exactly Morwani's inequality with q uniform on D_p and tau set to the point mass on y(x)-delta, summed over neurons (eta_theta = sum_i eta_{omega_i} by linearity).

The only difference: we use a point-mass tau at each offset instead of a uniform tau. That gives one inequality per delta, which the later coverage min over delta needs. The step is trivial and adds nothing as a result.

The paper's current wording already credits Morwani appropriately. The bib entry is correct: title, authors and ICLR 2024 confirmed.

Reviewers are likely to recognise three reformulations:

(1) **Max-margin under an l_q quasi-norm on Fourier coefficients (q < 1), with the exponent set by homogeneity.**
- Source: Gunasekar, Lee, Soudry, Srebro, NeurIPS 2018 (arXiv 1806.00468). I read Theorem 2a in the PDF.

- Theorem 2 covers L=2 and gives ||beta_hat||_1. The paper notes that p=2/L<1 is non-convex.
- The template is the same as ours: homogeneity gives an l_{2/depth} bridge penalty in frequency space, and that gives frequency sparsity.
- Differences: generic data, linear convnets only, no coverage or modular structure, no bound over all networks, no K* or log p count.

evidence: The transfer from the generating inequality to power sums and other penalties is a known general principle. Rajan & Tepedelenlioglu (IEEE TIT 61(4):1619-1628, 2015; arXiv 1302.5383) define the "ergodic capacity order" (Def. 1): X <=_c Y iff E log(1+rho X) <= E log(1+rho Y) for all rho >= 0. Their Property S1 states "X <=_c Y <=> E[g(X)] <= E[g(Y)] for all g in TBF", where TBF is the Thorin-Bernstein class g(x) = a + bx + int log(1+x/s) mu(ds) (their eq. 6). The proof of Property M1 (App. A, eqs. 28-31) matches ours step for step: take rho -> 0 for the linear term, then integrate log(1+t rho x) against a positive measure. Applied to the empirical measure of x (zero padding is allowed because a=0), it gives Remark "other penalties" verbatim, and Lemma cost at 0<r<1 is the case g = x^r. The class psi = cx + int log(1+xt) mu(dt) is exactly the Thorin-Bernstein functions vanishing at 0, which is Schilling-Song-Vondracek, Bernstein Functions, de Gruyter Studies in Math 37, Ch. 8 (1st-ed. TOC fetched; Ch. 8 starts p. 73). Lemma bernstein (the integral formula for x^r) is a standard Beta-integral representation. (i) Minimisers of sum v^{1/s} over P_p are vertices, and every minimiser is a vertex.

statement: A real exponential sum with N distinct exponents has at most N-1 real zeros (Rolle induction)
evidence:
The claim, in the appendix (app:shape (ii), sections/appendix.tex around line 156): a real exponential sum sum_k c_k e^{lambda_k u} with N distinct exponents, not all c_k zero, has at most N-1 real zeros. The paper proves it by Rolle induction.

This is classical. It is the generalized Descartes rule of signs (Laguerre): substitute t = e^u, and the number of zeros is at most the number of sign changes in (c_k), which is at most N-1. Equivalently, the functions e^{lambda_k u} form a Chebyshev (Descartes) system.

statement: At a vertex the active constraints have full rank, giving K independent tight offsets
evidence:
The proof step at appendix.tex:166 (proof of Prop. bottleneck) is a textbook LP fact. A point of a polyhedron in R^n is a vertex (extreme point) exactly when it is a basic feasible solution, meaning n of its active constraints are linearly independent. Source: Bertsimas & Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Linear Optimization (1997), Def. 2.9 (p. 50) and Theorem 2.3 (vertex = extreme point = BFS).

How this was confirmed:
- Wikipedia "Basic solution (linear programming)" was fetched. It gives the definition ("of all the constraints that are active at that vector, at least n of them must be linearly independent") and cites B&T 1997, Athena Scientific, p. 50, ISBN 978-1-886529-19-9.
- arXiv 2302.12364 was fetched and its text extracted. It states "basic feasible solutions are precisely extreme points (vertices) of the feasible set (Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, 1997, Theorem 2.3)". Its bib entry is "Athena Scientific, 1st edition, 1997. ISBN 1886529191".

Our argument is the standard basis-matrix argument (B&T Sec 2.3):
- The active bounds v_j=0 for j outside S are unit vectors supported outside S.
- So the active coverage rows, restricted to S, must have rank K, and the resulting K×K system is invertible.
The step is correct and nothing in the technique is new.

evidence: Paper (appendix.tex lines 198-214) uses three things. (1) The integral representation I_0(z) = (1/pi) int_0^pi e^{z cos th} dth, which is DLMF 10.32.1 (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.32, section 10.32(i)). (2) The Fourier coefficients of e^{z cos th} are I_k(z) >= 0. This is the Jacobi-Anger expansion DLMF 10.35.2, "e^{z cos th} = I_0(z) + 2 sum_{k>=1} I_k(z) cos(k th)" (fetched https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.35), and non-negativity follows from the power series in 10.25.2.
